description:
Read one clip: its elements (positions/sizes in canvas pixels), voiceover (text, voice, duration, voiceover_volume), background and transition. Pass `render` to also get a PNG of the frame.

ASK FOR WHAT YOU NEED. A full read is large — on a dense clip the per-word voiceover array and the element type_data blobs dominate it, and repeated full reads are the main way a long session runs out of context. `select` returns exactly the parts you name:

  select: ['elements.x','elements.y','elements.width','elements.height']   → geometry only, to fix a layout
  select: ['elements.name','elements.start_time','elements.end_time']      → a timing pass
  select: ['voiceover_words']                                              → word timings only, to sync visuals to narration
  select: ['elements.textdata','voiceover_words']                          → rewrite copy against the VO
  select: ['elements']                                                     → whole element rows, no words
  select: ['groups']                                                       → group rows only, to get a group_id for update_groups
  select: []                                                               → no JSON at all (pair with render for the PNG alone — smallest read)
  (omit select)                                                            → everything; fine for a first look, expensive to repeat

`render` is the other output, and it is separate from `select`: `select` shapes the JSON, `render` produces a PNG.

  render: {}                                     → the frame at t=0
  render: { timestamps: 2.5 }                    → the frame 2.5s into the clip
  render: { timestamps: [0.5, 2, 4] }            → those three moments as ONE labelled grid
  render: { timestamps: [...], layout:'separate'} → the same moments as full-size images (~4x the tokens)
  render: { save: true }                         → also uploads the frame and returns presigned_url
  render: { element_id: 'e1' }                   → just that animation, cropped, at four moments (a fast check)
  render: { filmstrip: true }                    → the whole clip, every element, as 12 frames in one image with a timeline of cues, actions and element starts/ends
  render: { animation: '@org/cast', entry: 'maya' } → that entry alone on this clip, nothing placed or saved
  render: { preview: '<token>' }                 → an edit_animation dry run, cropped, at four moments
  (a render of one animation also returns { warnings }: a glow cut at its box, text off its frame, frames near the limits)
  render: { element_id: 'e1', actions: [{name:'wave', start: 1}], cues: {reveal: 2} } → try settings, tracks, actions or cues without saving
  render: { max_width: 1280 }                    → a sharper frame when you must read small print
  select: [], render: {}                         → the PNG alone, no JSON (the default for a render of one animation)
  select: ['elements'], render: {}                → element rows AND the frame

A single frame renders 960px wide by default — legible for this design system and about half the tokens of a 1280 frame. A GRID defaults to 1280, because that is the width of the whole grid and a third of 960 would leave each cell unreadable. Either way `max_width` caps the image you get back; raise it only to read genuinely small print. For a render of one animation (element_id, animation + entry, preview) it sets the resolution the canvas is drawn at before the crop: each cropped cell of the sheet is at most 360px wide whatever you pass, so a higher max_width sharpens a small element but does not enlarge the sheet. To look closer, use layout:'separate' (full-size crops) or render the clip frame without element_id.

Omitting `render` renders nothing. `timestamps`, `layout` and `save` live inside it because they only mean anything for a render — there is no way to ask for them without asking for the image.

`element_ids` is the other axis: it picks WHICH element rows come back, independently of `select`. Combine them for the leanest read — e.g. element_ids: ['el_9'], select: ['elements.x','elements.y'].

Element shape: universal wrapper fields (id, element_type, name, x, y, width, height, start_time, end_time, rotation) plus type-specific data (textdata/shapedata/imagedata/videodata/zoomdata) plus an optional `keyframes` array when animated. Keyframes come back in the same flat wire shape add_elements takes — { timestamp, positionX?, positionY?, width?, height?, interpolation? } in canvas pixels — so you can round-trip read → edit → update_elements without reshaping.

An animation element that comes from an animation carries an `animation` block: { ref, entry, rev, live, updateAvailable, behind?, dependencyUpdates?, manifest: { params, actions: [{name, args, default_duration}], cues, presets, parts } }. That manifest is the vocabulary for update_elements' param_tracks / actions / cues, e.g. update_elements({updates:[{element_id, type_data:{cues:[{op:'set', key, t}]}}]}) — plan against it, not against the code. `behind: {rev, latest}` means the element still shows an older revision than the animation's latest passing one (placed elements stay on their revision until moved, unless they follow Live); `dependencyUpdates: [{animation, pinnedRev, latestRev, through?}]` means its animation imports, directly or through others, an older revision of another animation (`through` names the older one whose chain also re-pins it). The top-level `warnings` then says how many elements are affected and names the call that moves them: animation.update_uses('<animation>', {project}) or animation.update_dependents('<dependency>', {project}) in run_script.

Clip-level fields include `transition` (the current transition object — sibling of the update_clips `transition` arg; null if none) and `voiceover_words` (per-word timestamps, `{word, start, end, punctuated_word}` with start/end in SECONDS; null on clips with no transcription).

element_ids.description: WHICH element rows to return — all others are dropped, and [] returns none. Independent of `select`, which chooses the sections/keys. Use it to re-inspect just what you added or updated; most add_elements/update_elements already echo the element's resolved layout, so often you don't need this at all.

render.description: Render the clip as an image. Presence of this object IS the request to render — omit it and nothing is rendered. `{}` renders at t=0. Independent of `select`, which only shapes the JSON: pair `select: []` with `render: {}` for the PNG alone (smallest read). CHECKING YOUR WORK: pass `timestamps` with SEVERAL mid-clip moments, not the t=0 default — text and image elements have entry animations (a ~0.4s slide/fade by default), so at t=0 they have not arrived yet and a correct edit renders as an empty frame, while shapes have no entry animation and do show at t=0. That mix is what makes a single t=0 render actively misleading: some elements appear and others don't. A list comes back as one grid for about a quarter of the tokens of the same frames separately, so checking several moments is the cheap option, not the expensive one. `animations: false` draws everything settled if you would rather not pick moments at all.

actions.description: Action clips to try, [{name, start, duration?, args?}], element-local seconds; duration defaults to the action's default_duration. Replaces the element's clips for this render.

animation.description: With entry: render that animation entry on its own on this clip at its latest revision (or rev), without placing or saving anything. Pair with parameter_values, duration and timestamps as needed.

animations.description: Whether entry/exit animations play at this timestamp. Default true — the frame as the video will show it, which is what you want to judge motion. Pass false to draw every element settled at its final position and full opacity: use that to check COMPOSITION, because with staggered starts and short windows there may be no single timestamp at which nothing is mid-flight, and an element part-way through a slide reads as mis-positioned when it is fine.

cues.description: Cue times to try, key: seconds (element-local).

duration.description: With animation, or a preview without an element: how long it plays, in seconds (default its default_duration).

element_id.description: Render only this element over the clip's background, each moment cropped to its box, as one small sheet: the fast way to check one animation. Without timestamps it shows four moments across the element.

entry.description: With animation: the entry to render.

around.description: Center the window on a cue ('cue:land') or an action clip ('action:hop', by name or id) instead of from/to. On a whole clip, a cue several animations share is 'cue:land@<element name>'.

fps.description: Frames per second instead of a count, e.g. 8 over 2 s is 17, capped at 16.

frames.description: How many frames across the window, first and last included (default 12, max 16).

from.description: Window start, element-local seconds, or clip seconds for a whole clip (default 0).

seam.description: get_clip of a whole clip only: the cut from this clip into the next, as the player shows it: this clip's last second, its transition, and the next clip's first second, in this clip's seconds; takes frames, no window. Every cut of the film at once: get_project({render: {seams: true}}).

span.description: With around: the window's length in seconds (default 2 around a cue; the clip plus 0.5 around an action).

to.description: Window end, element-local seconds, or clip seconds for a whole clip (default the end).

filmstrip.description: See motion in ONE image instead of four moments: frames spaced evenly across a window (default 12 over the whole animation), in reading order, each labelled with its element-local time, with a thin timeline under each row marking the frames, cues (lines) and action clips (bars). Read pacing, easing and whether a beat lands on its cue from it. true for the defaults, or {from, to} / {around: 'cue:<key>' | 'action:<name>', span}, with frames or fps. Replaces timestamps. On get_clip without element_id, animation or preview it shows the whole clip, every element drawn, in clip seconds, and the timeline also ticks each element's start and end.

layout.description: Only meaningful when `timestamps` holds several. 'sheet' (default) tiles them into one image; 'separate' returns them full-size, which costs ~4x more — use it only when a grid cell is too small to judge.

max_width.description: Width in px of the image you get back: default 960 for a single frame, 1280 for a grid (the whole grid; a cell is about a third). An image costs about (w×h)/750 tokens and nothing is gained above 1568. On a render of one animation it is the resolution drawn before the crop; sheet cells stay at most 360px wide.

param_tracks.description: Keyframed settings to try, key: [{t, value, interpolation?}], t in element-local seconds. Replaces that key's track for this render.

parameter_values.description: Settings to render with, merged over the element's own (key: value).

preview.description: A preview token from edit_animation(dry_run: true): renders the unsaved code on its own as one sheet, cropped like element_id — the element the edit was about, or, for a dry run without an element, the entry alone on this clip. Nothing is saved.

rev.description: With animation: the revision to render.

save.description: Also upload the rendered image to S3 and return presigned_url, which you can pass as source_url to update_clueprint (files=[{path, source_url}]). Uploads ONE image, so it works with a single frame or a grid but not with layout:'separate' — there is one URL and several frames.

timestamps.description: Which moment(s) of the clip to render, in seconds (default 0). Pass several — [0.5, 2, 4] — and they come back as one labelled grid costing about a quarter of what those frames cost individually. Prefer several whenever you are checking rather than reading: entry animations mean no single moment shows everything, so one frame is usually the wrong question. A grid cell is a third of the width, so for small print pass a single number. Max 15; duplicates dropped, sorted into time order.

video.description: For people: also a short low-resolution MP4 of the same window (the filmstrip's, or the animation's first 10 s), returned as video_url, a link valid for an hour. You can't watch it: judge motion from the filmstrip.

select.description:
Ask for exactly the JSON you want, GraphQL-style. Omit for everything; pass [] for none.
  Sections: 'elements' (whole element rows), 'voiceover_words' (per-word VO timings; returns the key of the same name, holding `{word, start, end, punctuated_word}` with start/end in SECONDS — null on a clip with no transcription), 'groups' (group rows: id, name, parent_id, bounds_px, anchor_px, keyframes), 'busy' (generations still writing to this clip, as `[{entity_path, job_type}]` — EMPTY means nothing is pending, which is how you know a voiceover or AI image has landed; it is the same lock that would refuse your write, so a non-empty list also tells you what not to touch yet). Each section returns the key it is named after. Rendering is `render`, not a value here.
  Per-key: 'elements.<key>' projects element rows to just those keys (id is always kept). Keys: name, element_type, x, y, width, height, start_time, end_time, rotation, keyframes, textdata, shapedata, imagedata, videodata, zoomdata, codedata, avatardata, parent_id, dropShadows, animation. y_top is text-only and present ONLY when alignment is 'center' — the unambiguous TOP edge, which is exactly the case where `y` is NOT the top but the vertical CENTRE. To put that position back, send it as `y` with y_anchor:'top'.
  Examples: ['elements.x','elements.y','elements.width','elements.height'] to read geometry; ['elements.name','elements.start_time','elements.end_time'] for a timing pass; ['voiceover_words'] to sync visuals to narration; ['groups'] to resolve a group id for update_groups; [] with render:{} returns the PNG with no JSON (smallest read); ['elements.textdata','voiceover_words'] to rewrite copy against the VO.
  Mixing 'elements' with 'elements.<key>' returns whole rows. Use element_ids to choose WHICH rows — that is independent of this.

name: get_clip
